title: ARIA's CEO on Science Miracles, Valley of Death and UK Benefits
label: 8 Sep 2026 · ARIA evidence
summary: The Science and Technology Committee questioned Dr Kathleen Fisher, CEO of ARIA, about her priorities, how ARIA measures success, how it selects programme directors, its approach to commercialisation and UK economic benefit, its regional funding distribution, and how it compares to DARPA. Dr Fisher explained ARIA's high-risk, programme-director-led model, its focus on scientific breakthroughs and translation, and its efforts to spread funding across the UK, while acknowledging that more work is needed to change funding patterns.

speakers.label: Dr Kathleen Fisher
speakers.name: Dr Kathleen Fisher
speakers.role: Chief Executive Officer, Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA)

chapters.title: ARIA's scale and mission
chapters.takeaway: Dr Fisher explains that ARIA is now delivering across many programmes and that she will focus on growth and execution.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Dr Fisher. You took over as CEO of ARIA in February. Could you set out your key priorities and how your approach will differ as ARIA matures?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Thank you. When my predecessor spoke to you, ARIA was in its infancy. Now we have over 300 creators across 15 programmes and we're starting to see results. My time will be about growth and execution—getting the flywheel spinning at full velocity.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We'll spend the full £1.2 billion from the spending review, deliver the next cohorts of programme directors and activation partners, and see our existing programmes to possible extensions and exciting results.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: But success isn't measured by the number of creators or money spent. It's about three impacts: scientific breakthroughs that change how we think, societal and economic impact by crossing the valley of death, and a change in mindset—ARIA as a beacon of hope.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I spent seven years at DARPA and saw how effective that high-risk, programme-director-led model can be. I was blown away by how audaciously the UK set up ARIA, and I'm honoured to lead it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Could you pick a few existing programmes that excite you most, especially cross-cutting work with activation partners and the AI and science programme?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I'd love to. Let me start with the forecasting tipping points programme. It's developing low-cost sensors and models to monitor climate tipping points like the AMOC current and Greenland glacial melt.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: One company in Plymouth, Oshen, is making autonomous solar and wind-driven robots called sea stars. Instead of one big ship monitoring the ocean, a fleet of these can be deployed cheaply.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: They originally had one sea star, now five, and plan for 50 within a year. They were contracted by NOAA to monitor a hurricane, and they succeeded in transmitting data from inside category 5 Hurricane Humberto. Now they have contracts with five governments.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: That's an example of how ARIA works. Even if the programme falls short of its North Star, this small company could grow and deliver enormous technology.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Another example is our activation partner Amodo Design in Sheffield. They provide bespoke engineering to over 35 creators. One team needed batteries that work at minus 50 degrees Celsius for Greenland. The normal grant process would take 18 months; with Amodo they got a working modular battery pack in three months.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Those are two very interesting examples. Thank you.

chapters.title: Measuring success and allowing pivots
chapters.takeaway: ARIA tracks progress programme by programme, allows scientific pivots, and expects some failures as part of high-risk research.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: How do you define success and track progress across such an expansive portfolio in a light but effective way?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We start with the programme directors and the programme design. Each programme has its own milestones or metrics because success looks completely different for forecasting tipping points, AI safety, or precision neurotechnologies.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Programme directors meet with creators quarterly to check on science and translation. We track red, amber, green. If the science isn't going as expected, we can pivot—change the science a bit and shift red to amber or green. We don't treat that as failure because we're doing very hard science.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Annually, programme directors report to ARIA, and we bring in outside experts to review whether the programme is still worth doing or should pivot. Programme directors have terminated projects that aren't on track and repurposed funds. For example, in the safeguarded AI programme, one track was repurposed from verifying AI itself to using AI and formal methods to verify infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: Do the external reviews also check overlap with what others are doing, so you stay unique and blue-sky?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes. We always ask: would this work happen without ARIA? If it would, we shouldn't do it. We ask that during programme formulation and review. It's a needle to thread—if there's no work in an area, no one can do it; if there's too much, it's not appropriate.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: Overall, what does success look like for the portfolio? Matt Clifford said success is the overall programme's success, while many will fail. Do you share that?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Mostly, yes, but with nuance. Over 60 or 70 years, like DARPA, there will be punctuated massive successes—grand slams every 20 years or so. In between, there will be smaller wins, like Oshen, that are profitable and useful, even if they don't change everything.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: The grants are short—three years. Is that long enough? Do you follow up?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It's three to five years. The useful thing is that funding doesn't continue by default; it stops unless we proactively decide to continue. DARPA invested in AI for 60 years because over and over people decided it was still worth it. ARIA has mechanisms to double down, but each reinvestment is a fresh decision.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Also, working for ARIA can compress time. One researcher in Newcastle accomplished in a year what he planned for three because he went from 20% to 80% time, and his university supported that. His funding is extended, not cut.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: What about the people? If you have a star, can you keep funding them?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It depends on whether their research aligns with ARIA's purpose. ARIA doesn't have a long track record yet, but I could imagine that happening over time.

turns.speaker: Lord Duncan of Springbank
turns.text: If a project isn't going where you thought but has done useful stuff, how do you influence a pivot?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Absolutely. Programme directors talk to creators constantly. If the original vector isn't promising but a related one is, and it's still towards the North Star, that's a fine pivot. We're learning to write more flexible contracts so we don't have to rewrite them for every pivot, and we measure success separately from the contract.

chapters.title: Recruiting programme directors
chapters.takeaway: ARIA recruits programme directors in cohorts, seeking technical depth, breadth, judgment, entrepreneurial spirit, communication, leadership, resilience and feedback skills.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: Programme directors are critical. As you recruit your third cohort, what qualities are most important, and has that changed?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We're in the middle of recruiting cohort 3. We recruit entire cohorts so we can get balance across opportunity spaces and view a whole class of candidates at once, unlike DARPA's one-at-a-time approach. The deadline is 28 September, and we have over 1,200 applicants, up from 400 last round.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We look for technical depth to understand good science, technical breadth because programmes are interdisciplinary, and technical judgment to tell a well-grounded pitch from snake oil. We also need entrepreneurial spirit because ARIA isn't science for science's sake—we need to cross the valley of death.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Communication and leadership matter because programme directors don't do the technical work themselves; they convince and cajole others. They also need resilience because they'll be told their ideas are stupid or exciting. And they must take feedback well, because nobody comes with all these skills.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Cohort 1 was heavily academic, cohort 2 heavily entrepreneurial. For cohort 3 we want a balance. Cohort 1 allowed 80% time; cohort 2 required 100%; cohort 3 will go back to 80% to allow academics with PhD students. I've seen at DARPA that 80% can work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On the 1,200 applicants, what proportion are academics versus outside academia?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I don't know off the top of my head, but I can get you statistics. Maybe wait until after the 28 September deadline for the full pool.

turns.speaker: Lord Patel
turns.text: Does it matter whether they come from academia or industry?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The people matter hugely. Both can be successful. A mix is valuable because programme directors bond and talk to each other. We have a good mix across the first two cohorts and would like that in the third.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: Your predecessor said ideal projects are where there's violent disagreement—half think it's fantastic, half think it's rubbish. What do you think?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I wouldn't be as strong as 50:50. Zero people thinking it's good is a bad sign, and 100% is also a bad sign. If everyone agrees, it's probably too settled and the field will go there anyway. If nobody agrees, you probably shouldn't do it.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: That's a pretty sane answer. Thank you.

chapters.title: Funding models and autonomy
chapters.takeaway: ARIA uses different programme structures depending on the goal, and a new chief science and technology officer will help cohort 3 with sophisticated choices.

turns.speaker: Lord Winston
turns.text: Programme directors have great autonomy. How do they allocate funding, and what's your view on how research is best performed?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The right structure depends on the programme. In programmable plants, we allocated money up front because plants grow slowly. In enduring atmospheric platforms, the director overcommitted at the start to put more shots on goal, knowing some teams would be cut, though that means teams compete rather than collaborate.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Forecasting tipping points used a two-phase structure because they weren't sure what would work; phase 1 runs 18 months, then a second solicitation. Trust everything, everywhere ran a competition because the space moves fast and they wanted to see who would come. Competitions are hard to design so you reward the right things.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We recently hired a chief science and technology officer from DARPA who starts 1 October. He'll help cohort 3 with programme structures, including evaluation teams, which are common at DARPA and give directors a lever to make challenge problems easier or harder and facilitate translation.

chapters.title: Economic benefit and UK value capture
chapters.takeaway: Dr Fisher argues ARIA creates value by crossing the valley of death and that keeping IP with creators plus US activation partners with UK operations is the best route, while Lord Drayson presses on risks of UK benefits leaking abroad.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: ARIA is designed as a value-creation mechanism, but it has a mandate to bring economic benefit to the UK specifically. How is it doing that?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Value creation itself brings economic benefit. For example, precision neurotechnologies addresses disorders affecting one in six UK citizens and costing the NHS £4.1 billion a year. If we treat patients more economically and return them to the workforce, that's huge benefit without any profit.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: But we also have a value-capture role. We created a chief translation officer to identify impact paths. Our IP terms are designed to maximise benefit: we don't take IP, so creators keep rights and have a clean cap table when they start companies, making them more likely to get VC funding and commercialise.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Your example is global benefit, not specifically UK. In 2024, ARIA leadership said attempts to capture value for the UK could jeopardise attracting investment. Do you agree?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Crossing the valley of death is the first priority. If we cross it, we want to maximise UK benefit. We're creating an environment to make crossing it in the UK attractive—like venture cafés in London, Manchester and Edinburgh, and working with Fifty Years to help scientists become entrepreneurs and stay in the UK.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Why are some activation partners not based in the UK?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: When we made agreements with world-class deep-tech investors, the terms required them to establish UK operations and invest all the money in the UK. Yes, they're US companies, but they're focusing on the UK and bringing expertise.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: The UK doesn't have a problem attracting investment; it has a problem commercialising breakthroughs here. Should ARIA prefer UK investment partners?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: ARIA's role is producing companies with world-class technology and teams that want to stay in the UK. If UK investors want to fund them, great. If US investors do and the company stays in the UK, also great. The most important thing is that the company doesn't die.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Our Bleeding to Death report catalogued UK start-ups leaving. Do you see a risk that activation partners become acquisition partners, benefiting global investors rather than creating UK wealth?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I don't see that as a huge risk. I see the upside of leveraging their knowledge to produce world-class companies and maximise the chance of crossing the valley of death. It's not only ARIA's responsibility to make companies want to stay; the whole ecosystem must create those conditions. We're doing our part.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: ARIA doesn't retain IP. There are royalty arrangements, but concerns have been raised. Are you considering changing ARIA's approach to IP to ensure breakthroughs stay in the UK?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We're always reviewing policies. If we find one that serves our mission better, we'd adopt it.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: That's a very politician-like answer, Dr Fisher.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It happens to be true. We're constantly looking at IP policies, but our current assessment is that the policy Ilan described is correct. ARIA's best way to create value is to cross the valley of death by putting IP in creators' hands. Most creators are in the UK, so IP is in the UK. If licensed or sold outside, a royalty is due to the UK. If we find a better policy, we'll implement it, but our primary goal is value creation and crossing the valley of death.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: So you haven't considered changing ARIA's approach to IP?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We've talked about changing it, but those conversations concluded that our current policy is best for ARIA's mission.

turns.speaker: Lord Drayson
turns.text: Thank you for that clarity.

chapters.title: Chair conflict-of-interest episode
chapters.takeaway: Dr Fisher says the decision about Matt Clifford's role was for BIST, not ARIA, but she understands industry concerns and says board conflicts are declared and mitigated.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: Last week the ARIA chair, who has since resigned, was moving to Anthropic while retaining his position. That caused dismay given UK economic benefit and AI competition. What was ARIA's thinking?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It wasn't ARIA's decision. It was up to BIST to decide on mitigations. ARIA didn't have a role in that decision.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: Did you or the executive team consider how it might impact ARIA's perception or the industry?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It was a conversation between Matt and BIST. The appointment of the chair is under BIST, not ARIA's purview. We weren't involved.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: Did you receive feedback once it was announced?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes, I did receive feedback.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: Can you share it?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: The feedback was much along the lines you reported.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: What was your view on how to respond?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Those decisions were between BIST and Matt. It's up to them to decide what needed to be done.

turns.speaker: Lord Ranger of Northwood
turns.text: The concern is about confidence in UK AI businesses and conflict with large international firms. Do you accept that point?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I understand the concern, and ARIA wasn't consulted.

turns.speaker: Lord Patel
turns.text: Are there lessons learned about future chairs and conflicts of interest?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It's essential that the chair doesn't have conflicts that impede the agency. We choose board members for their expertise, and overlap with ARIA isn't uncommon. Members declare interests, which are published and monitored, and mitigations are put in place. ARIA has a code of conduct aligned with public bodies. You don't want board members who know nothing about the industry, so there's a judgment call.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The point is one of 100% transparency.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Indeed, that is exactly the point.

chapters.title: Regional funding and UK-wide talent
chapters.takeaway: Dr Fisher acknowledges ARIA isn't where it wants to be on regional spread, but is requiring programme directors to do UK-wide discovery and is refining data to track funding better.

turns.speaker: Lord Booth
turns.text: ARIA has been criticised for the share of funding going to the golden triangle. In 2025-26, 67% went there, barely changed from 66%. What steps are you taking to fund opportunity across the UK?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Our mission requires working with the best scientists, who are spread across the UK. I've mentioned Oshen in Plymouth, Amodo Design in Sheffield, Touchpoint in Sheffield, and a creator in Newcastle. But we're not where we want to be. The golden triangle has a dense concentration of world-class scientists, so it's not surprising they're well represented.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We now require programme directors to do their discovery across the UK, talking to a representative sample in all countries and regions. I've met with DCSAs in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and I'm scheduled for Wales. They've agreed to help identify scientists. I've also visited universities in Newcastle, Scotland and Northern Ireland to communicate how to work with us.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Programme directors can't get programme approval until they've demonstrated this. One director recently said they'd spoken to all but one region; we delayed approval until they did. We're taking it seriously, and the same applies to gender.

turns.speaker: Baroness Jones of Whitchurch
turns.text: The statistics aren't changing. It's good you're engaging, but the money still goes to the golden triangle. You need to find new talent, not just talk to people, or bids will come from the usual suspects.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: That's what the engagement is for—to find those people. We're also refining data collection, which currently only tracks primes. Primes have subs spread out, so prime contracts don't show where funding really goes. We're tracking applications at prime and sub level to see whether the problem is people not applying or not getting funding.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: At Newcastle, someone said they're serious about working with us, but part of the challenge is people not believing ARIA wants to work outside the golden triangle. Our funding covers 100% of costs, not 80%, so less well-funded universities aren't disadvantaged. Messaging is important for the long term.

turns.speaker: Baroness Jones of Whitchurch
turns.text: Latest stats show 15% of investment goes outside the UK. That's more than some UK regions. Are you reviewing that?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We definitely think about it, but the freedom to invest there is important. We ask if the UK has enormous scientific potential and whether we'll get strong proposals. It's unlikely all capability exists in the UK. We reserve up to 20% for non-UK research, but every proposal must cross a high bar—that it's a capability not in the UK and will enormously contribute. Sometimes non-UK companies relocate here. Normal Computing moved to London and invested 150% of their ARIA funding.

chapters.title: Understanding the research landscape and learning from DARPA
chapters.takeaway: Dr Fisher describes discovery tours, workshops and AI tools, and explains ARIA's similarities to and differences from DARPA, including mission, scale and procurement.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: How do programme directors understand the research landscape at a granular level?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: They start with an idea, read literature, use AI a lot, and talk to many people. People answer the phone for ARIA programme directors. They go on discovery tours; Ivan, for materials science, talked to people in every UK country and region.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: When satisfied, they publish a programme thesis to get open feedback, then run an invitation-only workshop. The discovery process often ends when no new names come up. Workshops bring together three or four disciplines that don't normally talk, and breakthroughs can happen. Then they write a programme approval document for a panel including the CTO, chief translation officer, CEO and outside experts.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: Those workshops include people outside the UK, whose view is valuable.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes, often world experts, including from outside the UK.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: On tipping points, you'd want places like Potsdam Institute.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Definitely. It's not just people in the UK.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: How do you compare ARIA and DARPA?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Both are high-risk, high-reward, programme-director-driven, project-based. DARPA's mission is national security; ARIA's is making the UK and world better through breakthrough science. DARPA does classified work, which adds friction. DARPA is bigger, older, and doesn't have to prove its existence; ARIA does.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: DARPA has the Department of Defense as a customer, but I think that's overblown. As director of I2O, I spent a lot of time strategising how to get results into the Pentagon. That translates to ARIA, where we must engineer translation.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: DARPA hires one at a time; ARIA hires in cohorts, though we'll hire individually sometimes. DARPA has another level of hierarchy. ARIA's scale is roughly the size of the office I managed at DARPA, with a significantly smaller budget.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: Public procurement is important for crossing the valley of death. Is there scope for a more active link between UK public procurement and ARIA?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Definitely. Every programme director has an impact plan. Some are early, some have entrepreneurs in residence teaching pitch decks. Sometimes we need to create a market. Advanced market commitments could help. For the Scaling Inference Lab in AI hardware, we funded novel hardware and then stood up rack compute with a government commitment to buy it. That's what our chief translation officer works on.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: Should BIST and the Treasury do more to encourage departments to engage early with ARIA?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: It depends on the programme. So far, government partners have been enthusiastic and helpful while preserving ARIA's independence. I'd welcome continued engagement as programmes reach the right stage.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: It's one thing you reaching out; another for them to actively get all parts of government to reach out to you.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Indeed. It's tricky because we don't want premature engagement, but when ready, we want active engagement with the appropriate parts of government.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: What lessons from ARIA can inform UKRI's changing landscape?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: A healthy UKRI is essential for ARIA. Our discovery process relies on a science base to build on. The UK is around third in research indices and per capita number one, thanks to UKRI investment. You can't have ARIA without UKRI doing blue-sky research and long-term infrastructure. ARIA does programmes and sprints; UKRI builds brick by brick. They're complementary. Before ARIA, the UK was missing a modality. I'm not an expert on UKRI, so I won't overstep.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: You're learning a lot. Do you see value in sharing that directly with UKRI?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Sure. I've met with Ian Chapman and heads of UKRI organisations multiple times. We have a lot to learn from each other.

turns.speaker: Lord Stern of Brentford
turns.text: I must observe that the UK's deep strengths come largely from a few hundred years of first-class universities before UKRI. That source is under financial threat. I wouldn't overdo the link to UKRI.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: I appreciate that information regarding UKRI and universities.

chapters.title: Avoiding overlap and using AI
chapters.takeaway: ARIA uses AI tools, talks to other funders, and relies on conflicted-free expert panels to check differentiation and avoid duplication.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: How do you avoid overlap with other trusts and foundations? I've been in workshops where most experts were from one country with self-interest. Are there alternatives to workshops?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We're experimenting extensively with AI. This summer we had a project called 'everyone is a dev'. programme directors use AI to read literature and challenge assumptions. I use multiple AI tools and tell them not to be sycophantic—to challenge me and give sources. We use these to supplement workshops.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Workshops have conflict-of-interest issues because attendees may be funding recipients, but they also recruit the creator base. Experts on review panels are expressly conflicted from receiving funding, so they're unbiased. We do our best to get unbiased opinions throughout.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: On overlap, some programmes directly overlap other large trusts and foundations.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We ask about differentiation among experts on panels who can't receive funding. Sometimes things seem similar but aren't. The digital olfaction programme is an example—an article compared it to specialised olfaction, but ours is a general-purpose e-nose. The programme director had already talked to everyone quoted. If we find something contradicts our thesis, we pivot or shut down part of the programme.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: What if the Gates Foundation had an almost identical call coming out?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: We'd talk to them—and we have been talking to the Gates Foundation, so I'm comfortable on that point. We'd do deeper discovery to figure out overlap, who the creators are, technical risk, and creator population. Funding two parallel efforts might be reasonable, or it might be double funding the same people, which wouldn't be appropriate.

turns.speaker: Baroness Willis of Summertown
turns.text: There's a network of foundations that talk to each other.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Yes, that is true.

chapters.title: Life sciences and data
chapters.takeaway: ARIA invests in life sciences through specific programmes, but its unit of deployment is programme directors, so it can't do everything; data ethics are taken seriously.

turns.speaker: Lord Patel
turns.text: Life sciences is a key pillar for UK growth, with NHS data as fuel. Do you see ARIA focusing on this area, given concerns about data use?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: ARIA has life science programmes. Precision neurotechnologies has two programmes on neurological and neuropsychological disorders with over £100 million invested. Programmable physiology has viral resistance and precision mitochondria, roughly another £100 million. So we do work in life sciences.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: But ARIA has $1.2 billion across all of science, which isn't much when spread out. We can only do things where we have programme directors—that's the unit of deployment. At DARPA, I wanted a programme on shutting down rogue AI but couldn't find a programme manager for two years. For ARIA to work in a space, we must hire a director there.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: On data, protections are always important. We take ethics and responsible practice seriously. If we stood up a programme on big medical data, we'd follow those practices and potentially research how to do it better.

chapters.title: Priorities and legacy
chapters.takeaway: Dr Fisher wants ARIA to deliver scientific and translation miracles, become a well-run organisation at steady state, and produce a breakthrough as impactful as DARPA's internet.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are your top priorities and what would you most like to look back on?

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: My priorities are delivering the science miracles, translation miracles and the beacon of hope. Long term, I want ARIA to create a breakthrough technology like the internet for DARPA, establishing ARIA firmly in minds. That will take time and is unpredictable. In the meantime, steady progress of important breakthroughs and meaningful translation for the UK.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Another contribution is growing ARIA from a start-up to a well-run organisation at full capacity, where programmes end at the same rate they're born. We're almost at steady state. An organisation of 10 people around a table operates differently from one where everyone no longer fits. Getting through that growth is important.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: ARIA is a place where people love to come, and I want to maintain that—not because it's the shiny new thing, but because people know they can make a tremendous difference. The people are critically important, across operational, communications, finance, procurement, programme directors and support staff.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Let me highlight programme director Brian Wang. Before ARIA, he started a company to create medication in advance of a pandemic. At ARIA, he's leveraging the innate immune system instead of the adaptive one. Adaptive vaccines must be crafted for specific viruses, which is why we need a flu vaccine every year. The innate system is more general purpose, and recent advances suggest we might sculpt and control it.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Brian's goal is protection lasting about three months. If successful, it would have enormous economic benefit—it could cure the common cold, so parents and workers miss less work. We'd want to commercialise it for UK value capture. It could also provide off-the-shelf treatment for the next pandemic, with national security applications. That delivers ARIA's mission.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A cure for the common cold is a great ambition.

turns.speaker: Dr Kathleen Fisher
turns.text: Of course, it's high risk, high reward. It most likely won't work exactly as envisioned, but no matter what, it will advance science.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Dr Fisher. You've been very helpful and informative. We wish you every success and will keep in touch. That concludes this session.
